summary: Defines the WebRTC threat model and analyzes the security threats to real-time communication in browsers.

plainLanguage.summary: WebRTC lets a web page place a call from your browser and send the audio and video directly to the other party. That is powerful, and it is also a risk: the page could start calls you never asked for, or reach your camera and microphone. RFC 8826 works out what has to be true before any of that can happen safely, and which attacks remain possible even then.

subtitle: What can go wrong when a web page is allowed to place calls from your browser, and what has to be true to keep it safe.

tldr.problem: A WebRTC call is set up by a web server that the user has never met, and the server controls both the call and the code running in the browser. That server can place calls, reach the camera and microphone, and see the call's addresses, so it can be used to spy on users or to attack their network.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8826 sets out the threat model and the requirements: consent is scoped to the origin and to the call, the far end must confirm it wants the traffic before any is sent, keys are exchanged automatically with forward secrecy, and the media must be protected against both reading and alteration.
tldr.outcome: The document is a threat model rather than a protocol: it says what a browser and a calling service must do to keep WebRTC safe, and it names the attacks that the design cannot prevent. A companion document describes the security architecture. The document is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 8826 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2021, and it has not been obsoleted. It is a threat model and set of requirements; the mechanism that meets them is described in RFC 8827, and the protocols themselves in RFC 8825.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Real-Time Communications on the Web Working Group has standardized protocols for real-time communications between web browsers, generally called WebRTC, described in RFC 8825. The major use cases are real-time audio and video calls, web conferencing, and direct data transfer. Unlike most conventional real-time systems, such as SIP-based soft phones, WebRTC communications are directly controlled by some web server.

In the simple system shown in the RFC, Alice and Bob both have WebRTC-enabled browsers and visit a web server operating a calling service. Each browser exposes standardized JavaScript calling APIs, implemented as browser built-ins, which the web server uses to set up a call between Alice and Bob. The web server also serves as the signalling channel, transporting control messages between the browsers. While this is topologically similar to a conventional SIP-based system, with the web server acting as the signalling service and the browsers as soft phones, control has moved to the central web server: the browser simply provides API points used by the calling service. As with any web application the server can move logic between the server and the JavaScript in the browser, but regardless of where the code runs it is ultimately under the server's control.

This poses security challenges beyond those of a conventional Voice over IP system, because it has to contend with malicious calling services. If the calling service can cause the browser to make a call at any time to any callee of its choice, the facility can be used to bug a user's computer without their knowledge, simply by placing a call to a recording service. More subtly, if the exposed APIs allow the server to instruct the browser to send arbitrary content, they can be used to bypass firewalls or mount denial-of-service attacks. Any successful system needs to be resistant to this and other attacks.

A companion document, RFC 8827, describes a security architecture intended to address the issues raised here.
sections.plainLanguage: The difference from an ordinary phone call is who is in charge. In WebRTC the web server sets the call up and also runs the code in your browser. A server that is hostile can place calls to a recording service without asking, or use your browser to reach things behind your firewall.

sections.title: The Browser Threat Model
sections.content:
The security requirements for WebRTC follow from the requirement that the browser's job is to protect the user. The core browser security guarantee is that users can safely visit arbitrary web sites and execute scripts provided by those sites. This includes sites hosting arbitrary malicious scripts, because it is trivial for attackers to divert users to sites of their choice: an attacker can purchase display advertisements that direct the user, automatically or by a click, to their site, at which point the browser executes the attacker's scripts. Browsers inevitably have bugs that cause them to fall short of this goal, but any new WebRTC functionality must be designed with the intent to meet the standard.

In this model the browser acts as a Trusted Computing Base, both from the user's perspective and to some extent from the server's. While HTML and JavaScript provided by the server can cause the browser to execute a variety of actions, those scripts operate in a sandbox that isolates them both from the user's computer and from each other.

Conventionally there are two kinds of attacker. Web attackers are able to induce a user to visit their sites but do not control the network. Network attackers are able to control the user's network and correspond to the Internet Threat Model of RFC 3552. In some cases a network attacker is also a web attacker, since transport protocols that do not provide integrity protection allow the network to inject traffic as if it were any other peer. TLS, and HTTPS in particular, prevent these attacks, but when analysing HTTP connections the traffic has to be assumed to be going to the attacker.

Access to local resources. The browser has access to local resources such as keying material, files, the camera and the microphone, but it strictly limits or forbids web servers from accessing those same resources. It is possible to produce an HTML form that allows file upload, but a script cannot do so without user consent, and cannot even suggest a specific file: the user must explicitly select the file and consent to its upload. Browsers are explicitly designed to avoid dialogs with the semantics of click here to bypass security checks, because research shows users are prone to consent in those circumstances. Some resources cannot be accessed from the browser at all: there is no way to run specific executables directly from a script, though a user can be induced to download and run them.

The same-origin policy. Many other resources are accessible but isolated. While scripts are allowed to make HTTP requests through the fetch API, when the requests are made to a server other than the same origin the script came from, they cannot read the responses. Cross-Origin Resource Sharing and WebSockets provide an escape hatch. The same-origin policy prevents server A from mounting attacks on server B via the user's browser, which protects both the user, for example from misuse of their credentials, and server B, for example from denial-of-service attacks. More generally it forces scripts from each site to run in their own isolated sandboxes. Interactions between them generally have to be mutually consensual and are limited to certain channels: multiple pages from the same origin can read each other's JavaScript variables, but pages from different origins, or even IFRAMEs from different origins on the same page, cannot.

Bypassing the policy. CORS is a response to the demand for mash-ups, in which a script from origin A uses resources from origin B. When a script from origin A executes a potentially unsafe cross-origin request, the browser instead contacts the target server to determine whether it is willing to allow cross-origin requests from A, and only then allows the request. WebSockets allow cross-origin establishment of transparent channels: once a connection has been established, the script can exchange any traffic it likes without framing it as HTTP request and response transactions. As with CORS, a WebSockets transaction starts with a consent verification stage. Designing a correct consent verification system is difficult, and vulnerabilities have been shown in the existing Java and Flash consent verification techniques and in a simplified version of the WebSockets handshake. It is important to be wary of cross-protocol attacks, in which the attacking script generates traffic that is acceptable to some non-Web protocol state machine. To resist this, WebSockets incorporates a masking technique that randomizes the bits on the wire.
sections.plainLanguage: The browser is the thing that protects the user, and it protects the user by making web pages behave like separate parties. A page from one site can ask another site for data, but only that other site can say yes, and the first page cannot read the answer. WebRTC has to work inside those rules, not around them.

sections.title: Access to Local Devices
sections.content:
Allowing arbitrary sites to initiate calls violates the core web security guarantee: without some access restrictions on local devices, any malicious site could simply bug a user. At minimum, it must not be possible for arbitrary sites to initiate calls to arbitrary locations without user consent.

For the user to make an intelligent decision about whether to allow a call, and hence whether their camera and microphone input is routed somewhere, they must understand either who is requesting access, where the media is going, or both. Two conceptual models cover most cases. The first is that the user is sending media to an entity because they want to talk to that entity. The second is that an entity, such as a calling service, asks to access the user's devices with the assurance that it will transfer the media to another entity. In either case identity is at the heart of the consent decision. The identity of the party the browser is connecting to is all that the browser can meaningfully enforce: if you are calling A, A can simply forward the media to C.

Consent to access local devices is largely orthogonal to consent to transmit data over the network. Device access consent is about protecting the user's privacy from malicious sites, while consent to send network traffic is about preventing the user's browser from being used to attack its local network. So communications consent is needed even if the site cannot access the camera and microphone at all, and the site needs to be concerned about camera and microphone access even if the data is sent back over plain HTTP.

Screen sharing. There has been demand for screen and application sharing, but the security implications are much harder for users to analyze intuitively than camera and microphone access. The most obvious threats are those of oversharing: the user may believe they are sharing a window when they are sharing an application, or forget they are sharing their whole screen with its icons and notifications. A less obvious threat involves the impact on the web security model. A key part of the same-origin policy is that HTML or JavaScript from site A can reference content from site B and cause the browser to load it, but cannot see the result unless explicitly permitted. If a web application is screen sharing the browser, that invariant is violated, with serious consequences: an attacker site could request screen sharing and then briefly open a new window to the user's bank or webmail account, using screen sharing to read the displayed content. A more sophisticated attack would open a source view window to a site and use the screen sharing result to view anti-cross-site request forgery tokens. These threats suggest that screen and application sharing might need a higher level of user consent than access to the camera or microphone.

Calling scenarios. A dedicated calling service, where the user has a relationship with a calling site and repeatedly makes calls on it, suits a long-term consent mechanism, such as installing an application to indicate permission. With any service where the user may use it to talk to many different people, there is a question about whether the user can know who they are talking to: if permission is granted to calling service A to make calls on the user's behalf, that is implicitly permission to bug the computer whenever it wants. Another simple scenario is calling the site the user is actually visiting, as in the click here to talk to a representative windows on shopping sites. The user's expectation is that they are calling the site they are visiting, but they are unlikely to want to give general consent, so a second consent mechanism is needed where consent is granted for the duration of a given call. Great care is needed in the design of that interface to avoid users clicking through, and the browser's own user interface chrome must clearly display elements showing that the call is continuing.

Origin-based security. The basic unit of web sandboxing is the origin, so it is natural to scope consent to the origin: a script from origin A must only be allowed to initiate communications, and hence to access the camera and microphone, if the user has specifically authorized access for that origin. Arguably the origin is not fine-grained enough. If consent is expressed solely in terms of the origin, then on any future visit to that site, including one induced through a mash-up or an ad network, the site can bug the user. Three counter-measures are considered. Individual consent asks the user for permission for each call. Callee-oriented consent only allows calls to a given user. Cryptographic consent only allows calls to a given set of peer keying material or to a cryptographically established identity. None is satisfactory in all cases: individual consent puts the user's approval in the interface flow for every call, which quickly becomes annoying and trains the user to click OK, and callee-oriented consent provided by the calling site does not work well because a malicious site can claim that the user is calling any user of its choice. Tying calls to a cryptographically established identity helps in some cases, and is convenient where the parties differ, but designing interface primitives that express this policy is challenging, and more so in multi-user calling cases.

Security properties of the calling page. Origin-based security secures against web attackers, but network attackers must also be considered. Suppose permission has been granted to a calling service at an origin with the HTTP scheme. On an unsecured network, such as a hotspot, browsing any HTTP site lets an attacker bug the user's computer: the user connects to an unrelated HTTP site, the attacker modifies the connection to inject an IFRAME or a redirect to the calling service's origin, and then forges the response from that origin to inject JavaScript that starts a call to the attacker. The attack does not depend on the media being insecure, and it need not be executed immediately: the attacker can infect the origin semi-permanently with a web worker or a hidden window. This risk is created by allowing calls at all from a page fetched over HTTP. Even if calls are only possible from HTTPS sites, if those sites include active content from an untrusted site, that content runs in the security context of the page, which could lead to compromise of a call even if the parent page is safe.
sections.plainLanguage: The browser must not let a page use the camera, the microphone or the network without permission, and the permission has to be tied to the site the user is on. Screen sharing needs more care than the camera, because a shared screen can show a bank account that the page itself was never allowed to read. And permission to a site is not enough on its own: the site also has to get the other end's agreement before sending anything.

sections.title: Communications Consent Verification
sections.content:
Allowing web applications unrestricted network access through the browser introduces the risk of using the browser as an attack platform against machines that would not otherwise be accessible to the malicious site, for instance because they are behind a firewall or NAT. To prevent this, and to prevent cross-protocol attacks, it is important to require that the target of traffic explicitly consents to receiving it. Until that consent has been verified for a given endpoint, traffic other than the consent handshake must not be sent to that endpoint.

Consent verification is not sufficient to prevent overuse of network resources. Because WebRTC allows a web site to create data flows between two browser instances without user consent, a malicious site could chew up a significant amount of a user's bandwidth without incurring significant cost, by setting up such a channel to another user. This potential denial-of-service vector reinforces the need for adequate congestion control in WebRTC protocols.

ICE. Verifying receiver consent requires an explicit handshake, and one is already needed for NAT hole punching. Interactive Connectivity Establishment, described in RFC 8445, includes a handshake designed to verify that the receiving element wishes to receive traffic from the sender. The site initiating ICE is presumed malicious, so for the handshake to be secure the receiving element must demonstrate receipt or knowledge of some value not available to the site, which prevents the site forging responses. With ICE, the STUN transaction IDs must be generated by the browser and must not be made available to the initiating script, even through a diagnostic interface. Verifying receiver consent also requires checking that the receiver wants to receive traffic from a particular sender at this time, since a malicious site may attempt ICE to known servers that are using ICE for other sessions. ICE provides this by using the STUN credentials as a form of per-session shared secret, known to the web application but also needed by the STUN-receiving element to be useful. There also needs to be a mechanism for the browser to verify that the target continues to wish to receive the traffic, because ICE keepalives are only indications; RFC 7675 describes the mechanism for providing consent freshness.

Masking. Once consent is verified there is still some concern about misinterpretation attacks. This does not seem to be of serious concern with DTLS, because the ICE handshake enforces receiver consent and there is little evidence of passive DTLS proxies of the type studied in the literature. However, because WebRTC can run over TCP there is some concern that attackers might control the ciphertext by controlling the plaintext input to SCTP, a risk only partially mitigated by the SCTP stack controlling the framing. In principle an attacker could exert some control over SRTP packets by using the WebAudio API and extremely tight timing control, and the primary risk seems to be the carriage of SRTP over TURN TCP; but SRTP packets have a very characteristic packet header, so it seems unlikely that any but the most aggressive intermediaries would be confused into thinking another application-layer protocol was in use.

Backward compatibility. A requirement to use ICE limits compatibility with legacy non-ICE clients, and it seems unsafe to remove the requirement for some check completely. All the proposed checks share the same feature: the browser sends some message to the candidate traffic recipient and refuses to send other traffic until that message has been replied to, and the message and reply must be generated so that an attacker who controls the web application cannot forge them, generally by containing a secret value that must be incorporated. Non-ICE candidates include STUN checks without ICE, and using RTCP as an implicit reachability check. In the RTCP approach the WebRTC endpoint is allowed to send a limited number of RTP packets before receiving consent, which allows a short window of attack, and some legacy endpoints do not support RTCP, so it is a more expensive solution for those endpoints, for which it would likely be easier to implement ICE. In the STUN approach the WebRTC endpoint can verify that the recipient is running some kind of STUN endpoint, but unless the responder is integrated with the ICE username and password establishment system, the endpoint cannot verify that the recipient consents to this particular call. If the systems are tightly integrated the issue does not exist, but that design is very close to an ICE-Lite implementation.

IP location privacy. As soon as the callee sends their ICE candidates, the caller learns the callee's IP addresses, and the callee's server-reflexive address reveals a lot about the callee's location. To avoid tracking, implementations may wish to suppress the start of ICE negotiation until the callee has answered, and either side may wish to hide their location entirely by forcing all traffic through a TURN server. In ordinary operation the site learns the browser's IP address, though it may be hidden by mechanisms such as Tor or a VPN. Because sites can cause the browser to provide IP addresses, this gives a mechanism for sites to learn about the user's network environment even if the user is behind a VPN that masks their address, so implementations may wish to suppress all non-VPN candidates for users on privacy-oriented systems.
sections.plainLanguage: Before any media is sent, the far end has to say yes, and the answer has to come from something the calling page cannot fake. ICE does that job: the browser makes up the secret, the page never sees it, and the far end has to echo something only the browser knows. The same handshake that gets through a firewall also proves the far end wants the call.

sections.title: Communications Security
sections.content:
It must be possible for the communicating parties to establish a channel that is secure against both message recovery and message modification, for both data and voice or video. The technology for providing this service, such as SRTP, DTLS and DTLS-SRTP, is well understood, but it has to be examined in the WebRTC context, where the threat model is different. Unlike a conventional SIP proxy, the calling service controls not only the channel between the endpoints but also the application running on the user's browser. In principle the browser could cut the calling service out of the loop and present trusted information directly, and get consent, but practice in modern browsers is to avoid this. In-flow modal dialogs requiring the user to consent to specific actions are particularly disfavored, because human factors research indicates that unless they are extremely invasive, users simply agree to them without actually consciously giving consent. So nearly all the interface will be rendered by the browser but under the control of the calling service, and this likely includes the peer's identity information.

Two classes of attack have to be distinguished. Retrospective compromise of the calling service is where the service was non-malicious during a call but is subsequently compromised and wants to attack an older call, often called a passive attack. A during-call attack is where the calling service is compromised during the call it wishes to attack, often called an active attack. Providing security against the first type is practical. It is extremely difficult to prevent a trusted but malicious calling service from actively attacking a user's calls, either by mounting a man-in-the-middle attack or by diverting them entirely, and that attack applies equally to a network attacker if the communications to the calling service are not secured.

Protecting against retrospective compromise. The attacker is assumed to have access to the protected media stream as well as full control of the calling service. If the calling service has access to the traffic keying material, as in Security Descriptions, a retrospective attack is trivial. This is particularly serious in the web context because it is standard practice to run extensive logging and monitoring, so it is highly likely that if the traffic key is part of any HTTP request it will be logged somewhere and subject to subsequent compromise. This makes an automatic, public key-based key exchange mechanism imperative for WebRTC, and that mechanism should provide forward secrecy. The signalling channel or calling service can be used to authenticate the mechanism. In addition, if end-to-end keying is used, the system must not provide any APIs to extract long-term keying material or to access stored traffic keys directly, otherwise an attacker who later compromises the calling service might use those APIs to recover the traffic keys.

Protecting against during-call attack. Even if the calling service cannot directly access keying material, it can mount a man-in-the-middle attack, telling Alice she is calling Bob and Bob he is calling Alice, while in fact acting as a bridge and capturing the traffic. Protecting against this requires positive authentication of the remote endpoint, such as explicit out-of-band key verification, for example by a fingerprint, or a third-party identity service.

Key continuity. A malicious calling service can present any identity it chooses, but it cannot produce a private key that maps to a given public key, so the browser could note a user's public key and raise an alarm when it changes. SSH uses a similar technique. This is far less useful in the WebRTC context. Much of the virtue of WebRTC, and of any web application, is that it is not bound to a particular piece of client software, so users will routinely use multiple browsers on different computers with different keying material, and will be alerted to key mismatches that are in fact completely legitimate, with the result that they are trained to click through them. It is also trivial to bypass such a mechanism, because the browser never gets the peer's identity from the user but from the calling service: the calling service only has to say that a call is to user Y where Y is confusable with X.

Short authentication strings. ZRTP uses a Short Authentication String derived from the key agreement protocol, designed to be compared by the users, for example read aloud over the voice channel or transmitted through an out-of-band channel, and if confirmed by both sides it precludes a man-in-the-middle attack. The intention is that the string is used once and key continuity is used thereafter. The SAS does not offer a practical solution to the problem of a compromised calling service. Voice cloning systems that mimic the voice of a given speaker are an active area of research and are already being used in real-world attacks, and are likely to improve. It is also unclear that users will actually use an SAS: the browser interface constraints preclude requiring the exchange before completing the call, so it must be voluntary, and many users simply ignore optional security mechanisms. Once users have checked the SAS once, key continuity is required to avoid checking it on every call, which is problematic for the reasons above, and users simply ignore indicators that calls are using unauthenticated keying material.

Third-party identity. The conventional approach to communications identity has been to have a third-party identity system, such as a public key infrastructure, authenticate the endpoints, but such mechanisms are too cumbersome for typical users. A new generation of web-based identity providers has been developed that uses web technologies to provide lightweight third-party authenticated transactions. It is possible to use systems of this type to authenticate WebRTC calls, linking them to existing user notions of identity, by using the third-party identity system to bind the user's identity to cryptographic keying material, which is then used to authenticate the calling endpoints. Calls authenticated in this fashion are naturally resistant even to an active man-in-the-middle attack by the calling site. There is one special case in which PKI-style certificates do provide a practical solution: calls from end users to large sites, which can easily get a certificate to authenticate their media traffic. This provides no additional security value when the calling site and the media peer are the same, but might be useful where third parties such as ad networks arrange calls without taking part in them.

Page access to media. Identifying the far endpoint is necessary but not sufficient for media security. In WebRTC, media flows into HTML5 MediaStreams that can be manipulated by the calling site, and if the site can modify or view the media the user is not getting the assurance they would expect from authenticating their peer. In many cases this is acceptable, because the user values site-based special effects over complete security from the site, but there are cases where users wish to know that the site cannot interfere. For that, it is necessary to provide features whereby the site can verifiably give up access to the media streams, verifiable from both the local and the remote side. Users must be able to verify that the person called has engaged a secure media mode, which requires cryptographically binding an indication of the local media access policy into the cryptographic authentication procedures. The use of such a mode is left to the discretion of the site, and the model requires that the remote party's browser be included in the Trusted Computing Base.

Malicious peers. One class of attack that is not generally tried to prevent is malicious peers. No matter what confidentiality measures are employed, the person being talked to might record the call and publish it, and no attempt is made to prevent them using voice or video processing to change their appearance. Digital Rights Management technologies exist to attempt to address these issues, but they are generally not compatible with open systems and WebRTC does not address them. Similarly, no attempt is made to prevent prank calling or other unwanted calls, which is in general in the scope of the calling site, though the strong authentication WebRTC offers may be useful as part of a defence.
sections.plainLanguage: The media must be unreadable and unalterable by anyone on the path, and the keys must be arranged so that a service which is broken into later cannot read an old call. What the design cannot do is stop a service that is broken into during the call from pretending to be the other party, because the page is what tells the browser who it is calling. The RFC looks at three ways to narrow that risk and finds each one weak on its own.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
Persistent endpoint identifiers can be a useful security feature, but they can also represent a privacy threat where the user wishes to be anonymous. WebRTC provides a number of possible persistent identifiers, such as DTLS certificates if they are reused between connections, and RTCP CNAMEs if generated according to RFC 6222 rather than the privacy-preserving mode of RFC 7022. To prevent this kind of correlation, browsers need to provide mechanisms to reset these identifiers, for example with the same lifetime as cookies, and the API should provide mechanisms to allow sites intended for anonymous calling to force the minting of fresh identifiers. IP addresses can also be a source of call linkage.

Any new set of API features adds a risk of browser fingerprinting, and WebRTC is no exception. Sites can use the presence or absence of specific devices as a browser fingerprint. The API needs to be balanced between functionality and the incremental fingerprint risk.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things can tie calls together over time: a certificate or an RTCP name that the browser reuses, and the IP addresses. To let a user stay anonymous, the browser needs to be able to start fresh identifiers on request, and the set of devices a page can see has to be kept small so that it cannot be used to tell one browser from another.

sections.title: Security Considerations and IANA
sections.content:
The RFC states that the entire document is about security, and defines no IANA actions.

The requirements it reaches are these. Arbitrary sites must not be able to initiate calls to arbitrary locations without user consent, and consent to access local devices must be scoped to the origin. Before any traffic other than the consent handshake is sent to an endpoint, that endpoint must have consented to receive it, and the STUN transaction IDs used for that handshake must be generated by the browser and never exposed to the initiating script. The media channel must be secure against both message recovery and message modification, and where end-to-end keying is used the system must not offer APIs that expose long-term keying material or stored traffic keys. The key exchange must be automatic, public-key based and provide forward secrecy, so that a calling service compromised later cannot recover an earlier call. The document also states that the calling service and the remote browser cannot both be trusted by the user, and that identity in a WebRTC call is fundamentally mediated by the calling service, which is why consent, and the security properties of the page that carries it, matter so much.
sections.plainLanguage: The document sets requirements rather than a mechanism, and it registers nothing. Its central point is that a WebRTC service is controlled by a web page, so the browser, not the service, has to be the one that checks permissions and that the far end agrees to the call.
